prompt: A set of functional dependencies says: A fixes B and C together; B fixes C; A and B together fix D. What is a minimal FD cover of this set: an equivalent set with single-attribute right sides, no unneeded left-side attributes and no redundant dependencies?

options.text: A fixes B; B fixes C; A fixes D
options.explanation: Correct. Split the right side, drop B from the determinant fixing D because A already derives B, then remove the direct A-to-C dependency implied by the chain through B.

options.text: A fixes B; A fixes C; B fixes C; A with B fixes D
options.explanation: Splitting right sides is only the first stage. B is still unnecessary in the determinant fixing D, and the direct A-to-C dependency is redundant.

options.text: A fixes B, C and D together (one rule)
options.explanation: This does not meet the singleton-right-side convention, and loses the independent rule that B fixes C.

options.text: A fixes B; B fixes C; B fixes D
options.explanation: Starting from B reaches only B and C. Making B fix D is a stronger, unsupported constraint.

workedExample:
1. **Split right sides:** A fixes B, A fixes C, B fixes C, and A with B fixes D.
2. **Extraneous left attributes:** in "A with B fixes D", A alone already reaches B (and then C and D), so B is unnecessary. The rule becomes "A fixes D".
3. **Redundant rules:** "A fixes C" follows from A fixing B and B fixing C, so drop it.
4. **Check nothing else can go:** without "A fixes B", A would reach only D; without "B fixes C", nothing reaches C from B; without "A fixes D", nothing reaches D. All three are needed.

Result: A fixes B, B fixes C, A fixes D. From A it still reaches everything, exactly as the original set did.

link.title: Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design

prompt: A set F of functional dependencies says: A fixes B; B fixes C; A fixes C. Two FD sets are equivalent when each implies every dependency of the other. Which of these FD sets are **equivalent** to F? Select all that apply.

options.text: A fixes B; B fixes C
options.explanation: Correct. The two-step chain through B supplies the omitted direct rule fixing C from A, and every rule in this set is in the original.

options.text: A fixes B; A fixes C
options.explanation: Here B determines only itself, so the original rule fixing C from B is lost.

options.text: A fixes B and C together; B fixes C
options.explanation: Correct. Splitting the combined right side recovers both rules from A, while the rule fixing C from B is retained.

options.text: A fixes C; C fixes B
options.explanation: This wrongly adds a rule fixing B from C, and cannot recover the original rule fixing C from B.

workedExample:
Two rule sets are equivalent when each implies every rule of the other. The original set is: A fixes B, B fixes C, A fixes C. The rule that decides this question is "B fixes C", because it is the only one starting from B.

1. **First option:** it keeps "B fixes C", and the chain A to B to C restores "A fixes C". Nothing new is added. Equivalent.
2. **Second option:** starting from B reaches only B, so "B fixes C" is lost. Not equivalent.
3. **Third option:** "A fixes B and C together" splits into the two rules from A, and "B fixes C" is kept. Equivalent.
4. **Fourth option:** starting from B reaches only B, so "B fixes C" is lost; and it claims "C fixes B", which the original never implies (starting from C there reaches only C). Not equivalent.

link.title: Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design
